chapters.title: One channel, many jobs
narration: Every one of this dome's 55 seams has a channel inside it. Air can go in through it, out through it, round in a loop, through a desiccant or past one, over a cold plate or a warm one. That is a lot of choices. This film works out which one to make, and when, from one number.

chapters.title: Inner skin, outer skin
narration: First, the word you were looking for. The line that runs from the centre of the dome straight outward is the radial direction. Through a wall it is the wall's thickness. In a seam it runs from the V's open mouth on the room side up to the ridge on the weather side. So the channel has two skins: an outer one that touches outside, and an inner one that touches the room. Put a Peltier plate on each and you can set the temperature of both.

chapters.title: A plate is a heat pump
narration: A Peltier plate is not a cooler. It is a pump that moves heat from one face to the other, and reversing the current reverses the direction. So the rule for both plates is simple: throw the heat to the side you want warmer. In winter, into the room. In summer, outside. The first film, The Wedge Dome Explained, showed the plate throwing its heat into the room. That is right in winter and wrong in summer.

chapters.title: Compare dew points, not humidity
narration: Now the rule the whole system runs on. Never compare relative humidity. Compare dew points. Outside air at minus 5 degrees and 60 percent sounds damp. Its dew point is minus 11.6. Inside at 21 degrees and 45 percent, the dew point is 8.6. Per kilogram, the damp-sounding air carries 1.6 grams of water; the room's carries 6.9. Bring it in, and it dries the dome.

chapters.title: Will it condense?
narration: The second question: will this air leave water on that surface? It will whenever the air's dew point is above the surface's temperature. So a condensing plate must be colder than the dew point. And every piece of wood must be warmer than it, with room to spare. This film keeps wood 3 degrees above the dew point of the air that touches it.

chapters.title: Fifteen to twenty degrees colder
narration: You asked: if the wood sits at the dew point and the metal channel is fifteen to twenty degrees below it, will the water go to the metal? Take a room at 21 degrees and 55 percent. Its dew point is 11.6. The middle of your range, 17.5 degrees under that, is minus 5.9. The plate freezes. Frost stops the water running and chokes the fins. So hold the plate 6 degrees under the dew point and never below 1: here, 5.6 degrees.

chapters.title: Plate first, wood second
narration: And the real answer: a colder surface somewhere else does not protect wood that is already at the dew point. Wood touching raw room air still gets wet. What protects it is the order. Send the air over the plate first. It leaves with a dew point of 7.6, so wood at 11.6 is now 4.0 degrees clear. One more rule: the cold metal must never touch the wood, or it chills the wood to its own temperature.

chapters.title: Seven modes
narration: That gives the channel its modes. Take outside air in. Push inside air out. Condense inside air on a cold skin before it leaves. Loop the seam's own air through the desiccant. Purge a wet seam with outside air and send it straight back out. Supply dried air and hold the room at a slight positive pressure. Or shut the exposed intakes in the rain. The loop and the purge never touch the living space.

chapters.title: The weathers we assumed
narration: To test the controller, here are the weathers from your table, plus one more. These are typical conditions, our estimates, not measurements from a site. Each one gets inside and outside temperatures and humidities, and the wet ones get a wood moisture reading at or over 19 percent, where lumber stops counting as dry.

chapters.title: What the controller chose
narration: And here is what the code chose, working only from dew points. Cold and dry: take it in. Hot and humid: dried supply only. Rain: shut. After rain, with dry air outside: purge the seam. Muggy outside with a wet frame: close the loop. All 11 weathers get the answer your table gives, and the film's own test fails if one ever does not.

chapters.title: The loop and the purge
narration: The two modes worth the extra plumbing are these. The frame loop takes the seam's air, dries it in the desiccant and sends it back: nothing thrown outside, nothing muggy pulled in. The purge takes dry outside air through a wet seam and straight back out. That needs two outside ports per circuit, and it means drying the frame is a separate job from ventilating the house.

chapters.title: The dome's levels, from the solver
narration: Now where each job goes. The solver's dome stands on five heights: 10 corners at the rim, 5 and 5 in a belt that zigzags between two heights, 5 round the crown, and the apex. The seams between them fall into five bands: 20 in the lower band, 10 in the belt, 15 in the upper band, 5 round the crown pentagon, and 5 to the apex.

chapters.title: The ring that cannot drain
narration: The slopes decide the jobs. The lower band's seams rise at 57 degrees, and water runs down them fast. The belt zigzags at only 8 degrees, but that zigzag has 5 low points, and each one is a natural drain. The pentagon ring round the crown is dead level. Water there stands in the wood. So that ring carries air, never water.

chapters.title: Condense low, drain at the rim
narration: Your idea of putting the plates on the first ring is right, and here is why. Condensate falls. A plate at the rim drops its water straight into a drain at one of the 10 rim corners, with no seam to travel through. The rain belongs outside, in a gutter at the rim. It should not come in through a seam higher up. Every foot of seam that carries liquid water is a foot of wood waiting for a leak.

chapters.title: Warm air rises
narration: Air has its own preference. Warm inside air wants to leave at the top, so take air in at the rim and let it out at the pentagon ring and the apex. But the pull is small. With the inside ten degrees warmer, the height of this dome makes 1.2 pascals. The barrier fan holds 4. The stack helps; it does not replace the fan.

chapters.title: Why the desiccant stays out of the seams
narration: Now the cartridge. Could you pack the beads into the seams themselves, round a ring, or over the top like a rainbow, a path of 32 feet? Push one seam's share of air, 13 cubic feet a minute, through one packed seam and the beads resist with 65,848 pascals. A small in-line fan manages about 250. At that, a packed seam passes 0.29 cubic feet a minute. The rainbow is longer still.

chapters.title: And it cannot be dried where it sits
narration: There is a second reason. A molecular sieve gives its water back only when it is hot: about 200 degrees. Even silica gel wants 120. The printed key softens at 80, and this film never sends air hotter than 60 through a seam. A desiccant in the seams could never be regenerated in place.

chapters.title: Two drawers and a gate
narration: So the desiccant lives in drawers, at the rim, where the channels come down. One drawer 30 centimetres square and 5 deep holds 2.9 kilograms of beads, and passes the whole dome's 18 cubic feet a minute at 20 pascals. Use two: one working, one being dried. The gate that picks between drawer and bypass should fall back to the bypass when the power goes, so air never stops.

chapters.title: What the desiccant will not do
narration: And the number that does not help. A frame that gets wet, over 19 percent, has 54 kilograms of water to lose to get back to 12. That is 93 drawer fills, and 56 kilowatt hours to regenerate them. The desiccant is for the weather when no air is dry enough. Drying a wet frame is the purge's job, on the next dry day.

chapters.title: The stove's heat, never its air
narration: The stove can help, but only through a wall of steel. A sealed exchanger on the flue warms clean air, and that air can dry the frame or regenerate a drawer. The smoke side never meets it. Keep the seam air under 60 degrees. Give the stove its own outside combustion air. And never let the stove push or pull the seam air, or a back draught puts smoke in the walls.

chapters.title: The layout
narration: So here is the layout. At the rim: 10 ports, the condensing plates, the drains and the two drawers. The lower band carries air up and water down. The belt's 5 low points drain it. The pentagon ring is the exhaust manifold: air only. The cap vents at the apex. Sensors inside, outside and in the seam read temperature and humidity, the wood's moisture, and the rain.

chapters.title: A correction: the cap never opens
narration: First, a correction. Earlier in this film, the stack chapter let the exhaust out at the pentagon ring and the apex, and the layout said the cap vents at the apex. That is wrong. A vent at the apex is a hole in the cap, at the place the weather hits hardest, with the frame right under it. The cap is one watertight layer, and it is never opened. Here is how the dome breathes anyway.

chapters.title: In at the crown, under the cap
narration: Warm air rises, and the warmest air in the room is also the wettest and the stalest: breath and steam, carried up. In a dome it collects at the crown. So a grille there, inside the shell and under the cap, takes the room's air into the seam channels, inside their printed keys. Holes through the cap above the rim: 0.

chapters.title: Down the seams, out facing the ground
narration: From the crown the air goes down. 50 of the dome's 55 seams fall all the way from the apex to the rim without climbing; the 5 level seams of the pentagon ring stay off the path. It leaves at the rim, through ports under the cap's brim that face the ground. Rain falls; an opening that faces down takes in only water that would have to climb. The dome needs 17.6 cubic feet a minute, and the five cap seams carry 4.2 times that at a quiet speed.

chapters.title: In winter the air falls by itself
narration: Here is why down is the right way. In winter the room's warm air rises to the crown. In the channel the exhaust gives its heat to the cold shell, gets heavier than the room's air, and falls. A warm column rising and a cool one falling make a loop that turns itself. At -5 degrees outside it pulls with 1.5 pascals and carries 100 percent of the need with no fan. In cool weather, 77 percent. In summer sun it runs backwards, and the fan does it all against 3 pascals, where a small fan pushes 250.

chapters.title: The water leaves by the same door
narration: When the channel is colder than the room air's dew point, the exhaust drops water inside the key: 0.24 litres a day at -5 degrees outside, 1.9 at -15. That water runs downhill, which is the way the air is already going, and out of the same ports. Sent up, it would run back against the air and pool. Sent down, nothing pools, and the wet air never touches the wood: it runs inside the key.

chapters.title: Two ways, both doors at the bottom
narration: The dome breathes both ways. Fresh air comes in through its own ports at the rim, facing the ground, and into the room low, past the drawers and plates. Stale air leaves from the crown, down the seams, and out at the rim. The room itself is the loop's rising leg. Run the two flows equal, and the room is neither pressed nor pulled, so no air is forced through the frame either way.

chapters.title: Where it stops working
narration: And where it stops. With the channel halfway between inside and outside, the outlets reach freezing below -21 degrees outside, and ice can close them: heat the outlet stubs, or run the exhaust through the rim drawers on those nights. A port under a snowdrift does nothing, so keep the ports above the snow line. Screen every one. And in summer the fan carries the whole need.

chapters.title: Seventy on the box
narration: Now the plates themselves. You bought one thermoelectric module, a TEC1-12706, for 20 dollars, and want 10 round the rim, one at each port, running day and night on the sun. The listing says 70 watts. Worked from the listing's own maxima, the most it can move is 50, and only with no temperature difference across it. Mounted here, hot face on a finned sink outside at 30 degrees, cold face in a room at 26 and 60 percent, it settles at 14.8 degrees, draws 4.6 amps, and moves 28 watts of heat for 65 watts of electricity, its fans included.

chapters.title: A correction: less water per watt
narration: A correction. The Seam Does Four Jobs and The Wedge Dome Explained counted 6 plates at 60 watts, making 0.35 litres of water per kilowatt hour. That yield was an assumption, and it was wrong. Solved from the module, the cold face is 2.9 degrees under the room's dew point, and only 32 percent of the heat it takes is water. The yield is 0.20 litres per kilowatt hour: a litre costs 5.0 kilowatt hours, not 2.9.

chapters.title: Slower is better, until it stops condensing
narration: Run a Peltier gently and it gets far more efficient: at 3 volts it moves 3.05 watts of heat per watt, at 12 only 0.51. But at 6 volts the cold face stops at 18.4 degrees, above the dew point, and the water stops. The most water per kilowatt hour comes at 9 volts. And the controller asks for the plate 6 degrees under the dew point, 11.6. At full drive the module stops 3.1 short, so chasing that setpoint just runs it flat out. Cap the drive at 9 volts instead.

chapters.title: A day of ten
narration: Ten at 12 volts, all day, on a humid day: 281 watts of heat out of the room, and 3.1 litres of water a day. Two people, their cooking and washing, and the fresh air put in 9.1 litres. The ring takes out about 35 percent. It helps; it does not keep up. And the hot faces must be outside: they throw 836 watts. Mounted the other way round, the ring is a 651 watt heater that drips.

chapters.title: Feeding it on the sun
narration: Running all day and all night, ten stations draw 651 watts: 15.6 kilowatt hours a day, 10.4 of them off a bank at night. From 4.6 peak sun hours, that takes about 4,508 watts of panels, and a 28.9 kilowatt hour bank to cover the night and one dark day. That is 16,347 dollars, for 200 dollars of modules. A small compressor dehumidifier takes out the same water for 1.7 kilowatt hours a day.

chapters.title: What to do instead
narration: So keep the plates for the job only they can do: drying a seam that will not dry itself in warm, still, humid weeks. Run them on daylight surplus, 6 hours a day: 3.9 kilowatt hours the array was making anyway, and 0.79 litres a day, with no extra battery. Cap the drive at 9 volts. And if the room itself needs drying or cooling for weeks, buy the compressor: the smallest window air conditioner moves 3.2 watts of heat per watt; the ring moves 0.43.

chapters.title: Dew point decides
narration: One rule runs all of it. Send air toward the structure only when its dew point is lower than the moisture you are trying to remove, unless you are sending wetter air to a cold metal surface built to collect and drain the water. The same seams, winter and summer, rain and sun.

chapters.title: Do the one thing
narration: If any of this was worth your time, send it to one person who can
carry it further than I can. That is the whole ask. One share from
somebody with reach does more for this than a month of me in a field
with a chainsaw.
